content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses agree on a settled core: the harlot symbolizes spiritual adultery — idolatry and covenant unfaithfulness to God, pictured as marital infidelity (Hosea 1–3; Ezekiel 16; 23; Jeremiah 2–3). They agree the referent of the great harlot of Revelation 17–18 is disputed, with imperial Rome as the dominant/most common identification, and apostate world religion, the papacy, and first-century Jerusalem (preterist) as recognized minority alternatives. Some also note the extension of harlot imagery to pagan commercial powers like Tyre and Nineveh.","book_summary":"The book defines the harlot as a covenant city or people unfaithful to its divine Husband while retaining the outward form of covenant. It identifies the Revelation harlot specifically and exclusively as Jerusalem — the great city spiritually called Sodom and Egypt where the Lord was crucified (Rev 11:8), branded with the name Babylon of the beast she rides — explicitly rejecting the Rome identification its own common-view note attributes to standard teaching. Opposite: Virgin.","consensus_core_identification":"Harlotry = covenant unfaithfulness/spiritual adultery against God; the Revelation harlot is a corrupt religious-political-economic system, most commonly identified as Rome, with Jerusalem as a recognized minority (preterist) alternative.","book_core_identification":"Harlotry = unfaithfulness by a party already in covenant (retaining its outward form); the Revelation harlot is literally Jerusalem, not Rome.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"Two boundary moves: (1) The book restricts harlotry to entities in covenant with God ('a covenant city or people unfaithful to its Husband'), which implicitly excludes or marginalizes the consensus's extension of harlot imagery to pagan cities like Tyre (Isa 23) and Nineveh (Nah 3) that were never covenant wives. (2) The book resolves the Revelation referent question that consensus leaves open, reclassifying the great harlot from Rome (the consensus's dominant identification) to Jerusalem — a position all four responses list, but only as a minority preterist alternative.","material_contradiction":"On the specific Revelation referent, the book asserts 'Jerusalem, not Rome,' directly contradicting the most common identification. However, this is a contradiction with one alternative inside an acknowledged open dispute, not with the consensus's settled core (harlotry = covenant unfaithfulness), which the book fully preserves and even sharpens.","rationale":"Reduced to minimum cores, both the consensus and the book identify the harlot as covenant unfaithfulness pictured as marital infidelity; the book's 'unfaithful to its Husband' formulation matches this exactly and its 'Opposite: Virgin' mirrors the consensus's harlot/Bride contrast. The book does not replace this central identification; it tightens it (covenant status required, outward form retained) and then commits to the Jerusalem referent for Revelation 17–18 — a referent explicitly catalogued by every blind response as an established preterist minority reading. Choosing a recognized minority option within an admittedly unsettled referent debate, while keeping the shared symbolic category intact, is boundary-level disagreement, not replacement of the consensus core. Hence REFINED rather than DIVERGENT.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue for DIVERGENT: the book's own common-view note frames the standard teaching as 'Rome, not Jerusalem,' and the book flatly denies that identification — accepting the book requires rejecting the dominant referent for the Revelation harlot. But since the consensus responses themselves declare the referent unsettled and list Jerusalem as a live alternative, the contradiction is with one branch of an open question, not with the consensus core. Conversely, one could argue MATCH since Jerusalem appears in the consensus alternatives; but elevating a minority alternative to the exclusive identification, plus narrowing harlotry to covenant parties only, is a material boundary change. The citation support could also be judged stronger: the Rev 17:18/11:8 'great city' linkage is the classic preterist argument, though the identity of the two 'great city' references remains an inference the printed verses do not by themselves compel.","confidence":"high"}
